requirements.requirement: node1 becomes the DNS resolver for the shared network, answering authoritatively for inventory.internal with node2's address, and forwarding all other queries upstream
requirements.summary: Ansible-applied VyOS config sets service dns forwarding listen-address 10.100.246.10, allow-from 10.100.246.0/24, upstream name-servers 1.1.1.1 and 9.9.9.9, and authoritative-domain inventory.internal -> a @ address 10.100.246.11 (cmd-8b074c5ed7ab4b0a). pdns_recursor confirmed listening on node1's LAN IP:53 (cmd-17e3367eef554a90). Functional verification from node3 shows inventory.internal resolving to 10.100.246.11 and example.com resolving via upstream forwarding (cmd-7812f057f46f4106), confirming both the authoritative record and upstream forwarding behavior end-to-end.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 are configured to resolve through node1
requirements.summary: Playbook used community.general.nmcli to set DNS to 10.100.246.10 and disable auto-DNS on both nodes; resolv.conf on both shows 'nameserver 10.100.246.10' (cmd-8b074c5ed7ab4b0a play 2 output, cmd-f7bbaac4c5544207, cmd-117562504ab843a1). Resolution of inventory.internal and example.com confirmed working through node1 on both clients, including after a subsequent reboot of each client, showing the configuration is durable.

An inventory.ini and playbook.yml were authored on the control node (node4) and executed with ansible-playbook, targeting node1 (VyOS) and node2/node3 (CentOS). The playbook was run successfully and re-run idempotently with no unexpected changes (cmd-8b074c5ed7ab4b0a, cmd-e18bc34d60e7478f).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on all managed nodes (node1-node4): pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Each node has a captured pre-restart boot_id, a reboot command, a post-restart boot_id that differs from baseline, and recovered functional state: node1 (baseline 9d3cb897 -> 92115f91, cmd-30df2e48f7d44cd8/cmd-54c9c6450c804eb4/cmd-c127eeeb7ade4e5a/cmd-9529a0ff5828431d, pdns-recursor active and config persisted in /config/config.boot); node2 (4cee4ea8 -> 8c759735, cmd-32d744e3dc6c48b2/cmd-c9a75bb34bc048a7/cmd-45184ac4644f4cb9/cmd-f7bbaac4c5544207, resolv.conf and resolution intact); node3 (71f12f87 -> c4a83014, cmd-898bae27b11a4e07/cmd-be6bde51cfc746f8/cmd-25e8fb65ef4d4fc5/cmd-117562504ab843a1); node4 (d3d54083 -> c754bd17, cmd-3a9664b7984945cd/cmd-2c1cd6c125674192/cmd-dd05b56488d540d7/cmd-e18bc34d60e7478f, full playbook re-run succeeded). Fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots (global:after_executor:*:boot-identity) independently corroborate all four changed boot IDs. One quality caveat: after_executor snapshots show a new 'NetworkManager-wait-online.service' failed unit on node2 and node3 post-restart that was not present at baseline; this is noted as a limitation but the core DNS client functionality was still verified working post-restart.

overall_summary: The executor successfully implemented node1 as an authoritative+forwarding DNS resolver for inventory.internal (pointing to node2) with upstream forwarding, and pointed node2/node3 at it via Ansible, with functional verification of both authoritative and forwarded resolution. The provider-wide restart protocol was completed for all four nodes with clear pre/post boot-identity evidence and recovered service/config state, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is moderate: an unused root SSH key and a leftover temp script remain on node1 from abandoned troubleshooting approaches, and two CentOS nodes show a new failed NetworkManager-wait-online unit after reboot that wasn't investigated.
limitations: NetworkManager-wait-online.service is shown as failed in the after_executor snapshot for node2 and node3 but was not investigated or explained by the executor; its impact on DNS resolution appears negligible based on the passing getent checks, but it is unexplained residual state from the restart cycle.
It cannot be fully confirmed from the trace whether /tmp/vyos_dns.sh and the root-added SSH key on node1 were ever removed, since no cleanup command targeting them was observed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most exploratory/failed commands during VyOS 'configure' session troubleshooting (e.g. cmd-780a2428975543f4, cmd-e9dfe81682c64237, cmd-9e948103768d4005, cmd-04e8916c9d344c3a, cmd-c7dddd8ce7a24f9c) did not persist any state (commits failed or were rejected) and are acceptable diagnostic churn. However, three residue items stand out: (1) cmd-6a5ab5c61e734be4 added the cluster SSH public key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1 (VyOS) to test root SSH login; this path was abandoned in favor of the vyos user + become, so the root key remains as unused, unreferenced access residue that was never cleaned up. (2) cmd-4fb937bc90804203 wrote /tmp/vyos_dns.sh to node1 as part of an SSH-based workaround that was superseded by the become-based Ansible task; the script file was not removed afterward. (3) The after_executor lifecycle snapshot shows a new failed unit, NetworkManager-wait-online.service, on both node2 and node3 that was not present at baseline, surfacing only after the mandated restart cycle; this was not explicitly diagnosed or remediated by the executor. None of these are destructive, broad, or security-weakening beyond the unused root key, and core task functionality was unaffected, but they represent unresolved residue.
